list.listitem: Most management recommendations are based on case reports, case series, or expert opinion. C
Children or adults ingesting less than 40 mg/kg can be observed at home. C
Experts recommend determining the amount of elemental iron ingested and the serum iron concentration, but little evidence exists for this practice. C

Deferoxamine (DFO) is an iron chelator, but no good human clinical study exists to support its use in iron overdose. DFO may cause serious adverse effects, and no clinical data on dosing are available to reduce these effects. C
No targeted treatment is necessary; treat with supportive measures and do not use ipecac syrup, activated charcoal, or cathartics. C
Iron overdose results in the generation of a large amount of free radicals, which can interfere with mitochondrial and other cellular processes.
Iron has a direct caustic effect on the GI mucosa, causing nausea and vomiting.
Obtain a history and objective proof, if possible, of the ingested product and the quantity.

Signs and symptoms will depend on the time since ingestion. Five phases of poisoning are described, mostly based on case reports:
GI phase: 30 minutes to 6 hours after ingestion: abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, hematemesis, melena, lethary, shock, and metabolic acidosis. Latent or relative stability phase: 6 to 24 hours after ingestion: GI symptoms resolve. In severe cases, this phase does not occur. Shock and metabolic acidosis: 6 to 72 hours after ingestion: Metabolic acidosis may occur due to iron in blood. Shock may be cardiogenic due to iron deposition in heart or hypovolemic from GI blood loss. Hepatotoxicity with or without hepatic necrosis: 12 to 96 hours after ingestion. Bowel obstruction: 2 to 8 weeks after ingestion.

Calculate mg of elemental iron ingested per kg body weight: 20 to 40 mg/kg of elemental iron is considered a small amount; 40 to 60 mg/kg is considered a moderate a mount; and >60 mg/kg is considered a large amount. Little evidence supports this distinction, and symptom severity may not be related to the amount ingested.
Patients who have ingested less than 40 mg/kg of elemental iron and are having mild symptoms can be observed at home.
Most experts recommend checking a serum iron level, but there is no evidence that knowing the serum iron level results in better outcomes (see Prognosis section) and may not correlate with symptoms.
Abdominal radiographs are unlikely to show radio-opacities if chewable iron tablets are swallowed.
One nonsystematic review found that the DFO challenge test was not helpful in determining prognosis.
CT with virtual iron content imaging or MRI can be used to assess liver iron content in patients with very elevated serum ferritin.
Address the ABCs (airway, breathing, circulation).
Do not give ipecac or activated charcoal without recommendation from a poison center or emergency department. No good evidence supports gastric lavage in iron overdose.

DFO is labeled for treatment of iron overdose, but it has little clinical data to support its effectiveness or to guide dosing. It may cause acute respiratory distress syndrome, hypotension, ototoxicity, and ocular toxicity.
Children with serum iron levels less than 500 mcg/dL can be treated safely without DFO, although this recommendation is based on a small case series.
Magnesium hydroxide administration does not reduce iron levels.
In the event of hepatic failure, liver transplant may be required.
Child-resistant vitamin containers do not appear to help, since many poisoning occur when children open these bottles or they are left open.
There has been a decrease in calls to poison control centers for iron poisonings since the FDA mandated unit-dose packaging of iron supplements in 1997.
Children with serum iron levels >500 mcg/dL may have more serious symptoms.
However, some children with higher levels will not have symptoms, and some children with lower levels will have profound symptoms.
